title: Give each call its own environment
starter:
type term =
  | Num of int
  | Param of int
  | Add of term * term
  | Call of term * term list

let rec eval (env : int list) (t : term) : int =
  match t with
  | Num n -> n
  | Param i -> List.nth env i
  | Add (a, b) -> eval env a + eval env b
  | Call (body, args) -> ignore args; eval env body
hints: The body must not see the caller's `env`. It should see a list built from the args.
Each arg is a term, so work it out first, with the caller's `env`: `List.map (eval env) args`.
The whole case is `| Call (body, args) -> eval (List.map (eval env) args) body`. The args use the old environment and the body uses the new one.

answer.code:
type term =
  | Num of int
  | Param of int
  | Add of term * term
  | Call of term * term list

let rec eval (env : int list) (t : term) : int =
  match t with
  | Num n -> n
  | Param i -> List.nth env i
  | Add (a, b) -> eval env a + eval env b
  | Call (body, args) -> eval (List.map (eval env) args) body
answer.explain: A call works out its args in the caller's environment, then runs the body in a new environment that holds only those values. The body's `Param 0` now means the first arg of this call. Running the body with the caller's `env` gives 101 for the second sample, because the body would read the caller's slot 0.
